tagline: A short stretch of U.S. 68 at Shakertown’s entrance
intro: Shakertown Road is a 2.4-mile stretch of U.S. 68 at the entrance to Pleasant Hill in Mercer County. Kentucky designated it a scenic highway and byway in 1995. The village, in Kentucky’s Bluegrass region southwest of Lexington, preserves 34 original nineteenth-century buildings and 2,800 acres of farmland.

Pleasant Hill’s Shaker community was active from 1805 to 1910. After the society dissolved, the property changed hands and uses, although elderly Shakers remained until Mary Settles died in 1923. In 1961, Lexington-area citizens led by Joseph Graves and Earl D. Wallace began a restoration effort. By 1964, the Friends of Pleasant Hill had secured a federal loan to purchase and restore the site.

From the west, the designated road begins 1.2 miles before the Shakertown entrance. The entrance is the central landmark of this short U.S. 68 corridor. Within the village, the Meeting House and Trustee’s Office belong to the story of its changing uses and rediscovery.

moments.title: Pleasant Hill
moments.text: Pleasant Hill’s Shakers used horses to pump water into a tower on high ground in the early 1830s. Pipes carried that water to kitchens, cellars and wash houses, where horse-powered washing machines reduced the work of laundering clothes and linens. The village already had large stone and brick dwellings, shops and stone sidewalks by 1825. Its engineering extended to farm work: an elevator moved grain to an upper mill floor, and a mechanical sheller processed corn. Thirty-four original nineteenth-century buildings survive at the village. Kitchen pumps had already been installed by 1825, before the later water tower system.

moments.title: Meeting House
moments.text: Pleasant Hill’s Meeting House became an automotive garage after the Shaker society dissolved. Its wooden floor had been built to withstand several hundred people dancing in worship, and it proved strong enough to support the vehicles driven inside. The building later changed use again, becoming a Baptist church.

moments.title: Trustee's Office
moments.text: Thomas Merton first visited Pleasant Hill in 1959 and recorded his look inside the Trustee’s Office in his journal. He described a double winding stair rising toward a dome on the roof. Merton was a Trappist monk at the Abbey of Gethsemani and had mentioned Pleasant Hill in his writing as early as 1949.
